t: Count Indices With Opposite Parity — Editorial
o: For each index i we must count how many later indices j > i hold a value of opposite parity to nums[i]. In Example 1, nums = [1,2,3,4]: index 0 (odd) sees evens at 1 and 3 → score 2; index 1 (even) sees odd at 2 → score 1; index 2 (odd) sees even at 3 → score 1; index 3 has nothing after it → 0. Example 2 shows a single element always scores 0. With n ≤ 100, an O(n²) double loop is trivially fast, but a suffix-count of even/odd values gives an O(n) solution just as easily.
k: Only parity matters: replace each number with nums[i] % 2.
The score of index i equals (number of opposite-parity elements strictly after i), which is computable with a running suffix count.
Traverse from right to left, answering each index before updating the counts.

a.i: For every index i, scan all j > i and count how many have different parity. This directly mirrors the problem definition and, given n ≤ 100, at most 10,000 comparisons — well within limits.
s: Create answer array of length n.
For each i from 0 to n-1, initialize count = 0.
For each j from i+1 to n-1, if nums[i] % 2 != nums[j] % 2, increment count.
Set answer[i] = count and return the array.
a.t: O(n^2) — two nested loops over all pairs (i, j).
a.sp: O(1) extra space besides the output array.

a.i: Maintain two counters — how many even and odd numbers appear strictly to the right of the current position. Sweep from right to left: record answer[i] as the counter of the opposite parity, then add nums[i]'s own parity into the counters. Each element is processed once.
s: Initialize evenCount = oddCount = 0 and an answer array of size n.
Iterate i from n-1 down to 0.
If nums[i] is even, set answer[i] = oddCount; otherwise answer[i] = evenCount.
Then increment evenCount or oddCount according to nums[i] % 2.
a.t: O(n) — one pass over the array with constant work per element.
a.sp: O(1) extra space besides the output array.

w: In an interview, mention the brute force first, then immediately propose the suffix-count sweep since it's barely more code and runs in O(n). Pitfalls: forgetting that j must be strictly greater than i (the last index always scores 0), and updating the parity counters before recording the answer would incorrectly include nums[i] itself. Edge cases: single-element arrays and arrays of all-even or all-odd values (all answers are 0). A likely follow-up: handle streaming updates or range queries, which would call for a Fenwick tree indexed by parity.
